title: Experience is not its own interpretation
point: A feeling, thought or attraction is real as an experience but doesn't settle who you are or who you love, so give patterns time instead of letting the feeling of the hour or anyone else decide, without throwing such feelings away either.
where: Practicing With Your Little One > What to Make of a Passing Feeling
quote: Feelings about yourself work the same way. "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche's pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably

title: Social practice should be reciprocal, not a performance test
point: Dates, confessions and other contact can turn into reassurance-checking when their hidden job is to prove you're lovable or normal; keep the contact, drop the test, and let it go both ways.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > First Social Connections, Done Right
quote: Neither of those approaches are the balance we're seeking, and both are treating the other person like they're your reassurance machine. I'm giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Instead, get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present.

title: Honesty is graded by earned trust
point: Privacy isn't fakery: people earn more of you by how they handle smaller truths and your no, a deep relationship that needs a fake happy self needs more truth or less depth, and acceptance alone doesn't prove love or trust.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
quote: And reaching out doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no.

title: Anxiety can protect without becoming an oracle
point: Anxiety may be trying to protect you without being right about what will happen, so hear it out without obeying it, and never test a prediction past a part's no to touch, sex, going deeper or an altered state.
where: Practicing With Your Little One > Journal With Each Hand > If it's anxiety
quote: Anxiety is often a part of you that's trying to protect you, making a guess about what's coming, like that people will laugh at you. Sometimes it's right, sometimes it's useful, sometimes it's not.
missing: That a part's no, or even hesitation, about sex, going deeper or an altered state is a stop and not a prediction to test; only touch is left ("if you don't want to be touched, say no now", under What to Make of a Passing Feeling). The subsection that said it is his cut X8 (Hear the Guard First's "If it says no, I'd listen" went with X1 too).

title: Match outcome claims to duration
point: Relief that fades and comes back is brief relief, not resolution or proof of what worked, and any tracking of it stays light enough not to become checking.
where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
quote: Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that's the endgame, it's just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy.
missing: The rule itself: a few hours of relief with the old feeling back later is relief, not a fix or proof of what worked, tracked lightly (jot what changed and how long it lasted, drop it if it feeds OCD patterns); that was If the relief doesn't last, his cut X10. The guide keeps only that calm is initial progress and, for pain, that a treatment that helps doesn't explain the cause.

title: Psychoactive adverse history changes planning
point: One psychotic-type or lasting bad reaction to a substance is enough to hold off retrying it until it's properly assessed and to be careful with similar drugs, without becoming an anti-drug rule or a reason to stop prescribed or dependence-forming drugs abruptly.
where: Altered States and Intensive Practice > When Escape Leaves Reality Behind > If a past trip went badly
quote: If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. Don't try again until you understand what would make it safe.

title: A healthy mind is not a perfectly clean mind
point: Unwanted, shameful or contradictory thoughts can come up without being your intent or identity; notice them, act on what you'd stand behind and let the rest go, as Buddhist training works by intention and repair rather than purity.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd > A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
quote: Minds come up with ugly and embarrassing stuff all the time, some of it the opposite of what you believe, and bodies do their own thing too. The Guide doesn't need to police your every thought. It notices the jingle and knows you didn't mean it, and that it isn't who you are.

title: Missing can become an optional cue for love
point: Missing someone can, if you like, become a cue for love or loving-kindness, without pushing grief away, assuming they receive it, or using it instead of contact, boundaries or action.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn't Begun > Missing Someone
quote: When you miss someone, let the ache be a cue for love. It doesn't have to become one more problem to solve, and pushing it away won't help.

title: Concentrated borrowed adulthood can be distributed
point: When one person carries many grown-up jobs for you, sort out which can become yours, which can be spread across people, services, routines or tools, and which belong in that relationship, without weakening a relationship you treasure.
quote: it might be mostly one person carrying a lot of it. Maybe you're picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you're struggling can be an enormous blessing. If it's more distributed, with various people you can count on for small parts, that can be more sustainable, even if it doesn't feel as deep.
missing: The inventory of what that one person carries: which jobs can become yours, which can go to friends, community, services, routines or tools, and which belong in the relationship, and the difference between missing them and practical collapse without them. His reorganization cut the sentence that carried the spreading ("Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works."); it isn't on the keep-as-is list.

title: Speak toward what is being built
point: Once reality is named honestly, aim your words at what you're building rather than at a feared identity you're denying, without glossing over grief, harm, anger, a no or who's responsible.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Speak Toward What You Are Building
quote: They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that's something you'd like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself "I'm not dependent." Well, now you're thinking about being dependent, just like that Pink Elephant.

title: Clarify support mode only when genuinely ambiguous
point: Listening, helping untangle, brainstorming or a mix are different kinds of support, so ask which is wanted when it's genuinely unclear, without making the question a ritual.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Ask What Kind of Company They Want
quote: Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: "Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, brainstorm, or...?" Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time, if it's obvious what they want.

title: Make the opening map explicitly leave the exercise
point: Each stage has to leave the exercise sooner or later: the inner adult becomes believable by starting to give the same care, protection or guidance in ordinary life, even in small ways.
where: Understanding Reparenting > Five Stages of Reparenting
quote: Whichever stage you're at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life.

title: Add the transfer mismatch under “When to Change the Strategy”
point: If the exercise goes well and ordinary life stays the same, the missing step may be transfer rather than a deeper meditation: notice what the adult did in there and do a small piece of it in daily life, without making it homework or a verdict.
where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
quote: And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn't as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion.
missing: The mismatch under When to Change the Strategy: a session can go well while life stays the same, which points to a missing transfer step rather than a failed or too-shallow meditation (notice what the adult did in there, do a small piece of it out here), with its limits (no homework after every session; weak carryover isn't proof it was fake). Its last trace there, "integrating the benefits into regular life (like texting a friend...)", was in X10.

title: Some real problems are blocked, not actionable yet
point: When every next step on a real problem is blocked by something outside you, waiting isn't avoidance; keep the condition that would reopen it in view and put your effort elsewhere instead of forcing a workaround.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd > A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
quote: Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else's end (you've asked, and followed up, and there's nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn't avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

title: Remember a stated support mode and avoid stale advice
point: Remember the kind of support someone said they want until they change it instead of re-asking (and don't guess it from stereotypes), and don't serve advice already given as if it were new.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Ask What Kind of Company They Want
quote: Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time, if it's obvious what they want. But as they say, "assume" makes an "ass" out of "u" and "me."
missing: Remembering the kind of support someone asked for until they change it, not guessing it from gender or another stereotype, and the stale-advice rule (advice already given, with nothing new changing it, gets a brief mention, not a re-run). He removed that paragraph in turn 106 ("it seemed extra"), before the keep-as-is list existed.

title: Memory support is not the same as reflective journaling
point: When reflective journaling makes things more confusing, a plain record (a dated note, what helped, a reminder, a next step, a voice note) keeps continuity without interpreting, and patterns can wait until later if they matter.
where: Practicing With Your Little One > Journal With Each Hand
quote: For some people, writing might make them feel more confused, especially at first, or nothing might want to be written. Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all.
missing: What the record can be (a dated note of what happened or what helped, a reminder, a next step, a voice note) and that a memory aid doesn't have to explain your life; those sentences went in his reorganization and aren't on the keep-as-is list.

title: One blocked problem should not block the whole life
point: One blocked problem shouldn't stall another that can move: choose the current focus by goal, impact, urgency and what can move now, and when everything feels scrambled, cut it to one organizing statement and one next step.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd > A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
quote: The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.
missing: Choosing the current focus by goal, impact, urgency, leverage and what can move now (the guide has only "the next sane step that fits your values"), and the overwhelm rule: one short organizing statement, one prioritized next step, and only a question whose answer would change it.
